recipe: Create a separate tsconfig.json for each runtime environment (server, DOM, web worker, test, shared code) and connect them with project references.
trigger_condition: Your application contains code that runs in multiple distinct environments (e.g., server-side, browser DOM, web workers, tests).
evidence: A single tsconfig.json can only represent a single environment, both in terms of what globals are available and in terms of how modules behave.

recipe: For unbundled browser ESM, TypeScript has no dedicated mode: use `"module": "nodenext"` and `paths` that map each URL import to local types, e.g. `"https://esm.sh/lodash@4.17.21": ["./node_modules/@types/lodash/index.d.ts"]`, plus `"*": ["./empty-file.ts"]` to catch unmapped bare imports.
trigger_condition: You are writing ES modules for the browser without a bundler or module compiler.
evidence: you can approximate them by using a combination of the `nodenext` ESM module resolution algorithm and `paths` as a substitute for URL and import map support.
_original_recipe: For browser ES modules without a bundler, use "module": "nodenext" combined with "paths" mappings as a substitute for URL and import map support.
_review_reason: too terse to act on; include the documented paths trick

recipe: When writing a library, use the strictest possible compiler settings, since satisfying those tends to satisfy all consumer configurations.
trigger_condition: You are authoring a reusable library rather than an application.
evidence: you can instead use the strictest possible settings, since satisfying those tends to satisfy all others.

recipe: Set "target" to the lowest ECMAScript version you intend to support to ensure emitted code doesn't use features from later versions.
trigger_condition: You are writing a library and need to decide on the target ECMAScript version.
evidence: Setting this value to the _lowest_ ECMAScript version that you intend to support ensures the emitted code will not use language features introduced in a later version.

recipe: In libraries enable `"verbatimModuleSyntax": true`: it rejects imports whose meaning would depend on the consumer's esModuleInterop setting, and rejects `export default` in modules emitted as CommonJS.
trigger_condition: You are writing a library and want to avoid module interop pitfalls for consumers.
evidence: This setting protects against a few module-related pitfalls that can cause problems for library consumers.
_original_recipe: Enable "verbatimModuleSyntax": true in library projects to guarantee import portability regardless of consumer esModuleInterop settings.
_review_reason: overstated ("guarantee"); state what it actually prevents

recipe: Enable "declaration": true in library projects to emit type declaration files (.d.ts) alongside output JavaScript.
trigger_condition: You are publishing a TypeScript library that consumers need type information for.
evidence: This is needed for consumers of the library to have any type information.

recipe: A bundled library that externalizes dependencies cannot get split module resolution; `moduleResolution: bundler` may accept imports of external deps that fail in Node. Prefer `nodenext` (or `node18`), or don't bundle the library.
trigger_condition: You are bundling a TypeScript library that mixes bundled first-party source with externalized third-party imports.
evidence: But TypeScript cannot be configured to use two different module resolution settings in the same compilation.
_original_recipe: When bundling a library with both first-party bundled code and externalized third-party dependencies, you must pick a single moduleResolution setting since TypeScript cannot use two different module resolution settings in the same compilation; choose between "bundler" (which may allow imports unsafe in Node.js) or "nodenext" (which may impose overly strict requirements on bundled imports).
_review_reason: over 40 words; state the guide's actual guidance

recipe: Consider not bundling your library to avoid the complexity of split module resolution between bundled and externalized code.
trigger_condition: You are designing the build pipeline for a TypeScript library and want to avoid module resolution conflicts between bundled and externalized parts.
evidence: Even better, consider not bundling your library.

recipe: When using dual-emit solutions, run tests and static analysis against all output bundles before publishing to catch type-safety issues that a single compilation cannot guarantee for both outputs.
trigger_condition: You are emitting both ESM and CJS outputs from the same source files using a single type-checking pass.
evidence: Running tests and [static analysis](https://npmjs.com/package/@arethetypeswrong/cli) against all output bundles before publishing significantly reduces the chance of a serious problem going unnoticed.
